analysis.one_liner: Raises federal payouts to $150,000 and expands coverage for people sickened by nuclear testing fallout and uranium mining.
analysis.headline: Despite 16 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and died there without a hearing, vote, or floor action when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand and extend the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, a federal program that pays people harmed by Cold War nuclear testing and uranium mining. It would raise compensation for downwinders to $150,000, add New Mexico's Trinity test area and Guam to the covered regions, extend eligibility for uranium miners, millers, drillers, and ore transporters through 1990, add kidney disease and more leukemia types to the covered illnesses, add medical benefits, and make it easier to prove claims with affidavits and tribal records. The bill never received any action after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Uranium miners, millers, core drillers, and ore transporters — including those who worked through 1990, ten years beyond current cutoffs — and their families; downwinders of the Trinity test in New Mexico and of testing in the Pacific, including residents of Guam, who are currently excluded; people in Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, and Utah living in affected areas; people who had claims denied or were paid at the old lower amounts, who could resubmit or collect the difference; and people already compensated, who would gain medical benefits. Many claimants are members of Native nations, and the bill directs the Justice Department to accept tribal records such as grazing permits and homesite leases as proof of presence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick uranium workers and nuclear-test downwinders

how_it_helps.text: Raises the fixed award for downwinder leukemia and specified-disease claims to $150,000, replacing the current $50,000–$75,000 amounts.

Adds New Mexico — home of the 1945 Trinity test, the world's first nuclear detonation — and Guam to the covered 'affected areas,' and extends the qualifying presence window to November 6, 1962, covering more exposure periods.
Extends uranium miner eligibility from mines operating through 1971 to 1990, and adds millers, core drillers, ore transporters, and remediation workers as covered occupations.
Adds kidney cancer, chronic renal disease, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia to the list of compensable illnesses.
Gives anyone receiving compensation eligibility for medical benefits on the same terms as Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program participants.

Lets claimants prove employment or presence with sworn affidavits from witnesses, and requires the Justice Department to accept tribal records — grazing permits, homesite leases, post office box records, letters from tribal leaders — as proof of presence, easing documentation barriers that fall hardest on Native claimants.
Allows denied claimants to resubmit up to three times and lets people already compensated claim the difference up to the new $150,000 amount, plus medical benefits.
Authorizes $3 million per year for epidemiological research on uranium mining and milling impacts on people who were not workers themselves, including miners' family members.
Extends the program's life from two years after enactment to 19 years, keeping the claims fund and filing window open.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, through the federal fund administered by the Justice Department. The bill sets no industry assessment or dedicated revenue: every $150,000 award, medical benefit, resubmitted claim, and top-up for previously compensated claimants comes from Treasury. Companies that mined and milled the uranium bear no new liability.

drawbacks.text: The cost is entirely open-ended federal spending: awards jump to $150,000, previously compensated claimants can collect the difference, denied claims can be resubmitted up to three times, medical benefits are added, and the fund runs 19 more years. Congress gets no offsetting revenue and no cost estimate is in the bill itself.

Accepting sworn affidavits — rather than payroll or government records — to establish employment and presence makes the program more accessible but relies more on witness testimony, which is harder to verify decades after the fact and could raise fraud-verification burdens for the Justice Department.

Some eligibility determinations remain discretionary: for miners with combined work histories, compensation depends on the Attorney General's determination of equivalent radiation exposure, which could produce delays or inconsistent outcomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a defined group of people with documented, catastrophic harm — cancer and organ disease linked to government-sponsored nuclear testing and the federal uranium procurement program — many of whom were excluded from the existing program entirely, including Trinity downwinders in New Mexico and Guam residents. The cost is real but ordinary: federal compensation spending spread over 19 years, with no industry levy or dedicated fund. The strongest good-faith objection is the price tag and looser proof standards, not the design's purpose. On balance this is a well-targeted compensation bill whose main weakness is that Congress never scored or debated it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day.
Sixteen senators cosponsored it — 13 Democrats, 2 Republicans (Mike Crapo and Jim Risch of Idaho), and 1 Independent — a bipartisan group drawn heavily from uranium-mining and downwinder states.
After the referral, the record shows no further action of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee with the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short term, the federal treasury kept the money — no new $150,000 awards, medical benefits, or claimant top-ups were paid during the 118th Congress. The people who lost were the sick uranium workers and downwinders the bill would have paid, many in New Mexico, Guam, and on Native nations, whose claims died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal treasury; sick claimants got nothing

for.name: Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of cosponsors from uranium-mining and downwinder states.

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, one of only two Republicans, lending it bipartisan cover in a Democratic-led Senate.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors (13 D, 2 R, 1 I)
for.role: Cosponsors including Heinrich, Kelly, Tester, Wyden, Bennet, Hickenlooper, Rosen, Smith, Merkley, Brown, Booker, Sinema, Risch
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none acted further, and the bill never reached a vote they could press for.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never held a hearing or markup on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll call; support was bipartisan, with 13 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsoring, and no recorded opponent.

industries.note: The bill costs these companies nothing: compensation for their former workers' cancers and kidney disease would flow from a federal fund, not from the companies. That leaves the health legacy of uranium operations socialized — taxpayers pay the workers while the industry avoids any liability — though the workers themselves would finally be paid.

industries.industry: Federal compensation programs (RECA and the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program)
industries.note: Both programs would pay out more: RECA awards rise to $150,000 with new medical benefits and a 19-year extension, and the Energy Employees program's Special Exposure Cohort would be opened to uranium miners, millers, drillers, and ore transporters from 1942 through 1990. The extra cost is the mechanism by which sick workers get paid.
